no_phone_transport.title: Silence on Public Transport
no_phone_transport.body: Do not talk on the phone or make video calls on trains, buses, or subways. It is considered highly disrespectful.
no_phone_transport.consequence: You may be scolded by other passengers or the conductor.
no_phone_transport.tip: If you need to take a call, step off at the next stop.

no_eat_walk.title: No Eating or Drinking While Walking
no_eat_walk.body: Eating or drinking while walking down the street or on transport (except Shinkansen) is considered bad manners.
no_eat_walk.tip: If you buy something from a vending machine or store, eat it nearby before continuing.

shoes_genkan.title: Take Off Your Shoes at the Entrance
shoes_genkan.body: You must leave your shoes in the genkan (sunken entrance area). Never step on tatami mats with shoes.
shoes_genkan.consequence: Severely offending the host or being asked to leave.

no_tattoos_onsen.title: No Visible Tattoos in Onsen
no_tattoos_onsen.body: Tattoos are historically associated with the yakuza in Japan. Many onsen and pools strictly ban them.
no_tattoos_onsen.consequence: Being kicked out of the establishment without explanation.
no_tattoos_onsen.tip: Search for tattoo-friendly onsen or use tattoo-cover patches.

no_touch_geisha.title: Do Not Touch Geisha or Maiko
no_touch_geisha.body: In areas like Gion, do not touch or block the path of geisha or maiko to take photos. They are professionals working.
no_touch_geisha.consequence: Local fines and being reprimanded by the police.
no_touch_geisha.tip: Take photos from afar without interrupting their path.

no_tipping.title: No Tipping
no_tipping.body: In Japan, you do not leave a tip in restaurants, taxis, or hotels. Good service is already included.
no_tipping.consequence: Staff will run after you to return the money.
no_tipping.tip: A simple gochisosama deshita (thank you for the meal) is enough.

ticket_machine_order.title: Order from the Machine Before Sitting
ticket_machine_order.body: Many ramen or fast-food places require you to buy your ticket from the machine at the entrance before finding a seat.
ticket_machine_order.consequence: Hindering the fast flow of the restaurant.
ticket_machine_order.tip: Carry cash; many older machines do not accept cards.

hashi_etiquette.title: Chopstick Etiquette
hashi_etiquette.body: Never stick chopsticks vertically into rice or pass food from your chopsticks to someone else's, as it resembles funeral rituals.
hashi_etiquette.tip: Use the chopstick rest when you are not using them.

no_blow_nose.title: Do Not Blow Your Nose in Public
no_blow_nose.body: Blowing your nose loudly in public, especially in restaurants or on transport, is considered disgusting.
no_blow_nose.tip: Go to the bathroom to blow your nose or do it discreetly.

kanpai_wait.title: Wait for Kanpai
kanpai_wait.body: Do not start drinking until everyone has their drink and someone says Kanpai (Cheers!). Also, do not pour your own drink; pour for others and let them pour for you.

no_touch_products.title: Do Not Touch Products Unnecessarily
no_touch_products.body: In traditional shops, craft stores, or food markets, avoid touching products if you are not going to buy them.
no_touch_products.tip: If you want to examine something, ask for permission first (mite mo ii desu ka?).

no_photos_restricted.title: No Photography
no_photos_restricted.body: Strictly respect no-photo signs, common in temples, shrines, and museums for spiritual or conservation reasons.
no_photos_restricted.consequence: Confiscation of the camera or expulsion.
no_photos_restricted.tip: If you do not see a clear sign, assume you cannot take photos inside temples.

trash_separation.title: Separate Your Trash
trash_separation.body: Japan has a strict waste separation system (burnables, plastics, cans, PET bottles).
trash_separation.tip: It is often easier to take your trash to your accommodation and throw it away there.

no_smoking_street.title: No Smoking on the Street
no_smoking_street.body: In most cities, smoking while walking down the street is prohibited. It can only be done in designated areas.
no_smoking_street.tip: Look for green Smoking Area signs.

bow_formal.title: Bow Slightly
bow_formal.body: The standard greeting is a bow. A simple nod is sufficient for foreigners.
bow_formal.consequence: The lack of a bow is not serious for foreigners, but doing it scores many points.
bow_formal.tip: Do not combine a bow with a handshake unless the local initiates it.

wildlife_monkeys.title: Jigokudani Monkey Etiquette
wildlife_monkeys.body: Do not touch or feed the wild macaques. Avoid direct eye contact as they perceive it as a threat.
wildlife_monkeys.consequence: Monkeys may become aggressive, scratch or bite, and steal your belongings.
wildlife_monkeys.tip: Keep a safe distance of at least 2 meters and keep all food sealed in your bag.

sumimasen.usage: The most useful word. Use it to call a waiter, apologize, or pass through.

arigatou.usage: To thank services, purchases, or favors politely.

wakarimasen.usage: Useful when spoken to in Japanese and you do not understand.

eigo.usage: Always ask this before speaking English.

ikura.usage: Pointing at an object you want to buy.

okaikei.usage: To ask for the bill. Make an X sign with your index fingers.

hitori.usage: Hold up one or two fingers when entering a restaurant.

bejitarian.usage: Caution: many Japanese do not consider fish broth (dashi) as meat.

niku_nashi.usage: More specific than saying vegetarian to ensure no derivatives.

toire.usage: Essential in stations or large streets.

arerugii.usage: Combine it with the ingredient, e.g., piinatsu arerugii desu (peanuts).

oishii.usage: Saying it out loud in a restaurant will make the chef very happy.

arigatou_mashita.usage: Perfect to say when leaving a store or restaurant.

densha.usage: Pointing at a train on the platform to avoid taking the wrong one.

byouin.usage: To ask for urgent medical help.
